### Some people believe that online lessons should replace most classroom teaching in secondary schools. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Online teaching can make schoolwork available beyond a particular classroom. However, replacing most classroom lessons would change more than the location of a screen. I support using digital lessons more widely, but I disagree that they should replace most classroom teaching in secondary schools.

One advantage of online lessons is flexibility. Students has access to materials without to travel to school, which can be useful during a temporary absence. A teacher could record a difficult explanation so that learners can pause it and return to an unfamiliar step. This may help them to studying at a suitable pace rather than copy notes while struggling to follow the speaker. A single successful online lesson proves that digital teaching is better for every student. Lessons that are more easier to revisit can also support a later classroom discussion, provided that the materials match what the class is learning.

Nevertheless, access to a recording is not the same as participation. Some students may share a device with relatives or lack an reliable connection. Others need a teacher to notice confusion before it becomes a larger problem. In a classroom, a short conversation can reveal that a learner has misunderstood the question rather than the formula. Online support should be provide, but the school would also need a practical way for students to ask questions and receive individual attention. Simply posting more videos does not ensure that these needs are met.

For these reasons, schools should combine digital resources with planned classroom work. Teachers could use recordings for review and reserve face-to-face time for discussion, feedback and activities that benefit from direct cooperation. The balance should depend on the task and students’ circumstances. Online teaching is a useful option, but replacing most classroom contact would require stronger evidence than the success of one lesson.

Reviewing a missed explanation can help a student identify the exact step that remains unclear. Students can also prepare specific questions before a seminar instead of asking the lecturer to repeat an entire topic.

Listening again does not necessarily reveal whether the learner can apply the idea independently. For this reason, a course should include short tasks that require students to use the material, and tutors should explain how recordings fit into the weekly schedule. Students who are absent for a legitimate reason should not be treated as lazy simply because they need this resource.

On balance, recordings are valuable when they provide another route to understanding and support informed questions. Universities should protect that benefit while maintaining opportunities for discussion and practice. Attendance policies may differ between courses, but the design of the learning activities matters more than assuming that the presence or absence of a recording determines how seriously every student studies.

units.student_markdown:
### Some secondary schools require students to wear a uniform. Do the advantages of this policy outweigh the disadvantages?

School uniforms create a shared appearance, but a common appearance do not automatically create a fair school. I believe uniforms can have modest practical advantages, although these advantages outweigh the disadvantages only when the policy is affordable and flexible.

A uniform can simplify the decision about what to wear each morning. It may also make differences in fashionable clothing less visible during the school day. If the school offers several comfortable option, students can chose items that suit the weather and the activities they will do. One school with a uniform had no reported argument about clothing, so uniforms prevent every form of bullying. A sensible policy could reduce one source of comparison, but it would still need to work alongside clear expectations about how students treat one another.

The main difficulty is the cost of a compulsory purchase. A family may already owns suitable clothes but be asked to buy particular items from a single supplier. Replacing a damaged jacket can create pressure, especially if a student is punished for arrive in a different one. Schools should consider the financial burden and allow practical alternatives while a replacement is arranged. It is also important to listen to students who find an item uncomfortable or unsuitable for a particular activity. Consistency should not prevent staff from responding reasonably to individual needs.

Overall, a uniform can be useful as a limited organisational tool. Its value depends of the details of the policy, not merely on the fact that students look alike. ### Some secondary students repeatedly postpone long homework assignments until the last evening. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could schools take?

Long assignments can become difficult before the actual writing or calculation begins. Some secondary students repeatedly wait until the last evening, even when the deadline was announced early. This may results from uncertainty about the task and from unrealistic planning. Schools can address both causes without assuming that every delay is simple laziness.

One cause are not knowing how to begin. A student may read a broad instruction and understand the topic but remain unsure what should the final product contain. Starting then feels like making a large decision with little information. Teachers could show an example of the required structure and ask students to identify the first manageable action. Giving every class a checklist will eliminate all late homework. A checklist is most useful when students understand why its stages matter and can ask questions when their own task does not fit the example exactly.

Another cause is underestimating the time needed. Students may plan only the final writing session and forget research, preparation or check. Several subjects may also set deadlines in the same week. Schools could coordinate larger assignments and include a small intermediate submission, such as a plan or one worked example. This would allow teachers noticing confusion before the final deadline and give students experience of estimate the remaining work. The intermediate task should be small enough to support progress rather than become another large assignment of its own.

Overall, delaying work may reflect unclear starting points and weak estimates of time, although circumstances differ between students. Clear examples, opportunities to ask questions and realistic intermediate stages can reduce these problems. Schools should review how students use the support and adjust it when necessary. The purpose is to make independent planning more achievable, not to replace every student’s judgement with a rigid schedule.
